title: IPv4 subnetting: twelve questions
purpose: A check on prefix lengths, masks, network and broadcast addresses, usable ranges and summary routes.
intro: Work each one out on paper or in your head. Usable host counts follow the usual rule for subnets of /30 and shorter: every address in the block except the network address and the broadcast address.

questions.text: What is the subnet mask for a /26 prefix, in dotted decimal?

options.explain: That is /18. The 192 sits in the third octet, which gives 18 network bits, not 26.
That is /25: one bit set in the last octet, worth 128.
26 network bits leave 6 host bits. The last octet has its top two bits set: 128 + 64 = 192.
That is /27: three bits set in the last octet, 128 + 64 + 32.

questions.text: How many usable host addresses does a /27 subnet have?

options.explain: 14 is the usable count for a /28, which has 4 host bits.
5 host bits give 32 addresses. Taking away the network address and the broadcast address leaves 30.
32 is the total number of addresses in a /27. The network and broadcast addresses cannot be given to hosts.
62 is the usable count for a /26, which has 6 host bits.

questions.text: A host has the address 192.168.10.77/26. What is the network address of its subnet?

options.explain: That would be the network if the prefix were /24. A /26 splits the last octet into blocks of 64.
A /26 has blocks of 64 in the last octet: 0, 64, 128, 192. 77 falls in the block that starts at 64.
76 is not a block boundary for /26. The boundaries are multiples of 64.
128 starts the next block, which holds 128 to 191. 77 is below it.

questions.text: What is the broadcast address of the subnet that contains 172.16.5.130/25?

options.explain: 127 is the broadcast address of the lower /25, which holds 0 to 127. 130 is in the upper half.
128 is the network address of the upper /25: the first address in the block, not the last.
A /25 splits the last octet into 0 to 127 and 128 to 255. 130 is in the upper block, whose last address is 255.
That is the broadcast address of 172.16.0.0/16. The prefix here is /25.

questions.text: What is the first usable host address in 10.20.30.96/28?

options.explain: 96 is the network address itself. It names the subnet and is not given to a host.
The first usable address is one above the network address: 96 + 1 = 97.
110 is the last usable address in this /28, one below the broadcast address.
111 is the broadcast address. The block runs from 96 to 111.

questions.text: What is the last usable host address in 192.168.4.0/22?

options.explain: That would be right for 192.168.4.0/24. A /22 spans four /24 blocks, from 192.168.4.0 to 192.168.7.255.
A /23 starting at 192.168.4.0 would end there. A /22 is twice that size.
A /22 covers 192.168.4.0 to 192.168.7.255. The last usable address is one below the broadcast address.
That is the broadcast address of the /22: the last address in the block, which is not given to a host.

questions.text: A subnet must hold 50 hosts. Which is the longest prefix, meaning the smallest subnet, that fits them?

options.explain: A /24 has 254 usable addresses. It fits, but it is four times the size of the smallest block that does.
A /25 has 126 usable addresses. It fits, but a /26 also fits and is smaller.
A /26 has 62 usable addresses, the smallest block that holds 50. The next size down, /27, has only 30.
A /27 has 30 usable addresses, which is too few for 50 hosts.

questions.text: Which of these addresses are in the same /27 subnet as 192.168.1.100?
questions.help: Tick every one that applies. The item is correct only with every right address and no wrong one.

options.explain: 95 is the broadcast address of the block before, which holds 64 to 95. The block holding 100 starts at 96.
The /27 that holds 100 runs from 96 to 127, so 97 is inside it.
126 is the last usable address of the block 96 to 127, so it is inside.
128 is the network address of the next block, which holds 128 to 159.

questions.text: A /24 network is divided into /28 subnets. How many subnets does that give?

options.explain: 4 is the number of bits borrowed, 28 minus 24. The number of subnets is 2 to the power of that.
8 would be the count for /27 subnets, with 3 bits borrowed.
14 is the number of usable hosts in each /28, not the number of subnets.
Four bits are borrowed, and 2 to the power of 4 is 16 subnets, each with 16 addresses.

questions.text: Which wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask 255.255.240.0?

options.explain: Subtract each octet from 255: 255 minus 240 is 15, and 255 minus 0 is 255.
The last octet of the mask is 0, so its wildcard is 255, not 0.
16 is the block size in the third octet for this mask. The wildcard value is one less: 15.
The third octet has not been inverted. 255 minus 240 is 15.

questions.text: 10.1.0.0/16 is divided into /21 subnets. Which subnet contains the address 10.1.9.200?

options.explain: That block covers 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.7.255. The third octet of the address is 9, which is past it.
A /21 has a block size of 8 in the third octet: 0, 8, 16 and so on. 9 falls in the block that starts at 8, which covers 10.1.8.0 to 10.1.15.255.
9 is not a multiple of 8, so 10.1.9.0 is not a /21 boundary. It is an address inside 10.1.8.0/21.
That block starts at 10.1.16.0, which is above the address.
A /23 covers only two of the four /24 blocks: 192.168.8.0 and 192.168.9.0.
Four consecutive /24 blocks that start at a multiple of 4 make one /22: 192.168.8.0 to 192.168.11.255.
A /21 covers eight /24 blocks, 192.168.8.0 to 192.168.15.255, which is twice what is asked.
A /20 starting at 192.168.0.0 covers 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.15.255: sixteen /24 blocks.
